Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is being used increasingly to detect DNA sequences for food quality testing for GM content, microbial contamination, and ingredient content. However, food processing often results in DNA degradation and therefore may affect the suitability of PCR or even DNA sequence detection for food quality assurance. This paper describes a novel approach using quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR) to estimate the extent of DNA degradation. With use of two maize endogenous nuclear sequences, sets of four qPCR assays were developed to amplify target sequences ranging from <100 bp to approximately 1000 bp. The maize nuclear sequences used encode chloroplastic glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase and cell wall invertase. The utility of the qPCR approach for quantifying the effective concentration of maize DNA that is needed to amplify variable length DNA sequences was demonstrated using samples of maize cornmeal cooked in water for variable times, extrusion products developed using different barrel temperature and torque settings, and a range of food products from supermarket shelves. Results showed that maize DNA was substantially degraded by a number of processing procedures, including cooking for 5 min or more, extrusion at high temperatures and/or high torque settings, and in most processed foods from supermarket shelves. Processing also reduced the effective concentration of DNA sequences capable of directing amplification of the <100 bp assays as well, particularly after popping of popping corn or extrusion at a combination of high temperature and torque settings. The approach for quantifying DNA degradation described in this paper may also be of use in disciplines where understanding the extent of DNA degradation is important, such as in environmental, forensic, or historical samples. fetched_contents.text: The Quality of DNA Isolated from Processed Food and Feed via Different Extraction Procedures Abstract The extraction of DNA is a critical step for species identification by PCR analysis in processed food and feed products. In this study, eight DNA extraction procedures were compared—DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit, DNeasy mericon Food Kit, chemagic DNA Tissue 10 Kit, Food DNA Isolation Kit, UltraPrep Genomic DNA Food Mini Prep Kit, High Pure PCR Template Preparation Kit, phenol—chloroform extraction, and NucleoSpin Food—Using self-prepared samples from both raw and heat-processed and/or mechanically treated muscles and different types of meat products and pet food (pork, beef, and chicken). The yield, purity, and suitability of DNA for PCR amplification was evaluated. Additionally, comparisons between the effectiveness of various extraction methods were made with regard to price, and labor- and time-intensiveness. It was found that the DNeasy mericon Food Kit was the optimal choice for the extraction of DNA from raw muscle, heat-treated muscle, and homemade meat products from multiple and single species. Keywords: DNA yield, meat products, polymerase chain reaction, DNA degradation, food analysis, food authenticity 1. Introduction Authenticity of species origin in food and feed products is important for law enforcement and for the protection of consumer health, as well as for economic and religious reasons. Total accuracy is not always guaranteed by labeling. For the identification of species in processed food products, an analytical approach must be used. Most analyses target proteins or DNA molecules which are extracted from tissues [1]. As the heating or canning process (121 °C, 15 min, 200 hPa) causes protein denaturation [2], DNA is a more suitable molecular marker for species authentication. In fact, DNA is also degraded into small fragments during the thermal process, but these are still detectable [3]. Moreover, DNA is largely unaffected by tissue source or sample damage [4,5]. However, fragment size is a limiting factor for the subsequent PCR [6]. Thus, DNA-based analytical methods represent a crucial approach for species identification in raw and highly processed meat products due to their high thermal stability and their very low detection limits. PCR and real-time PCR proved to be fast, reliable, and sensitive methods for species identification in foods and feeds with complex compositions [7,8,9,10,11,12,13,14]. Sequences of mitochondrial [15,16,17] and genomic DNA [18] were reported to be targeted as markers. The critical step in these approaches is the extraction of high-quality DNA in sufficiently large quantities from heterogeneous food matrices. Due to the fact that raw muscles are subjected to different treatments during the manufacturing process (high temperature, high pressure, addition of certain ingredients, etc.) which considerably influence the quality of DNA [19,20,21,22], it is necessary to individually optimize DNA isolation procedures for each type of food product. fetched_contents.text: Quantification of DNA fragmentation in processed foods using real-time PCR Analytical Methods Quantification of DNA fragmentation in processed foods using real-time PCR Highlights * • A real-time PCR method to quantify the degree of DNA fragmentation was developed. * • An indicator value “DNA fragmentation index” was created to express the degree of DNA fragmentation. * • Abstract DNA analysis of processed foods is performed widely to detect various targets, such as genetically modified organisms (GMOs). Food processing often causes DNA fragmentation, which consequently affects the results of PCR analysis. In order to assess the effects of DNA fragmentation on the reliability of PCR analysis, we investigated a novel methodology to quantify the degree of DNA fragmentation. We designed four real-time PCR assays that amplified 18S ribosomal RNA gene sequences common to various plants at lengths of approximately 100, 200, 400, and 800 base pairs (bp). Then, we created an indicator value, “DNA fragmentation index (DFI)”, which is calculated from the Cq values derived from the real-time PCR assays. Finally, we demonstrated the efficacy of this method for the quality control of GMO detection in processed foods by evaluating the relationship between the DFI and the limit of detection. Abbreviations ; DFI, DNA fragmentation index ; FAM, 6-carboxyfluorescein ; GMO, genetically modified organism ; IPC, internal positive control ; ITS, internal transcribed spacer ; ; ; PCR, polymerase chain reaction ; ; TAMRA, carboxytetramethylrhodamine ; Keywords DNA ; Fragmentation ; Processed food ; Real-time PCR ; Genetically modified organisms Introduction DNA-based food testing is performed widely using molecular biological techniques, such as the polymerase chain reaction (PCR). In particular, processed foods are subjected to PCR testing in order to detect, for example, contamination with genetically modified organisms (GMOs) (Huber et al., 2013, Mano et al., 2009, Nakamura et al., 2013) or the unintended presence of food allergens (Poms et al., 2004, Tanabe et al., 2007). With respect to consumer awareness and protection, it is important to test processed foods as they are the end products in the food supply chain. During the food manufacturing processes, food materials are altered in various ways using physical, chemical, and/or biochemical factors. DNA fragmentation can result from physical force, heat, alkaline pH, and enzymes (Chen et al., 2005, Klein et al., 1998, Quirasco et al., 2004, Vijayakumar et al., 2009). It has been reported that DNA fragmentation affects the results of PCR analyses (Chen et al., 2007, Yoshimura et al., 2005). For example, a quantitative assay for GMOs previously generated different results for raw material and processed foods (Gryson, 2010, Xing et al., 2015, Yoshimura et al., 2005). Processed foods comprise multiple types of food components, and DNA extraction from the sample matrix is indispensable as a first step in the testing procedure. However, successful DNA extraction from processed foods is difficult because of the complexity of food matrices. DNA extraction from processed foods often yields insufficient quantities of DNA and/or the PCR reaction can be inhibited by residual impurities in DNA extracts. Therefore, accurate and robust approaches for analyzing processed foods using PCR and elaborate quality control methods are needed. Despite this necessity, PCR analyses of processed foods are commonly conducted in the same manner used for unprocessed foods. The DNA yield in the extracted DNA is typically measured by UV-spectrometry at 260 nm or the fluorescence intensity of an intercalating agent (Matsuoka et al., 2001). If a sample comprises multiple components, taxon-specific real-time PCR can be used to quantify DNA exclusive to a specific target organism. To determine if a PCR reaction is inhibited by contaminants, we can use the internal positive control (IPC) reaction as described previously (Mano et al., 2011). In the IPC reaction, a small amount of DNA with an artificial nucleotide sequence is added to the reaction mixture with an extracted DNA sample, and a PCR reaction targeting the artificial sequence is used to determine if PCR reactions are inhibited in a given sample. In contrast, there is no standard technique to evaluate DNA fragmentation in processed foods. Chiueh, Chen, and Shih (2002) reported that DNA degradation occurred in heated maize samples and confirmed that they exhibited DNA degradation based on end-point PCR analysis of the zein gene. Murray, Butler, Hardacre, and Timmerman-Vaughan (2009) developed multiple quantitative real-time PCR assays targeting the lectin1 gene. These techniques can compare DNA degradation between similar types of samples; however, the applicability of each method is limited to a specific type of plant. Furthermore, these approaches are not capable of quantifying the extent of DNA fragmentation. To provide a more comprehensive evaluation of DNA fragmentation, we developed and investigated a methodology that would be applicable to a wide range of food products and allow for the quantification of DNA fragmentation as a numerical value. In this study, we evaluated DNA fragmentation using a series of real-time PCR assays to amplify DNA fragments of different lengths (Fig. 1a). During food processing, breaks in DNA are expected to occur in a random manner; therefore, the copy number of longer PCR products is likely to decrease. Therefore, we expected that the difference in quantification cycle (Cq) values calculated from the various real-time PCR assays would reflect the degree of DNA fragmentation (Fig. 1b). fetched_contents.text: The Challenges of DNA Extraction in Different Assorted Food Matrices: A Review - Sajali - 2018 - Journal of Food Science Introduction Consumers’ choices of food products are mainly influenced by their religion; Islamic and Jewish communities forbid pork in their diet (Kim, Yoo, Lee, Hong, & Kim, 2016), whereas Hinduism forbid consumption of beef (Bonne & Verbeke, 2008). In addition, lifestyle, diet, and health issues such as allergy contribute to the consumer's choices of food products (Ballin, 2010). Similarly, taste and flavor also play important roles in food selection. For instance, much of the world's population prefer beef over buffalo meat (Hossain et al., 2017). Escalating numbers of food forgery cases worldwide has created awareness for the need for detecting and authenticating food constituents. Mislabeling of food, for instance, has threatened the consumer's trust of products. For example, the European horsemeat scandal in 2013, sparked concerns about the meat composition declared on products. Moreover, a report published by the Food Safety Authority of Ireland found samples of commercial beef products contained a range of percentages of horsemeat (Salihah, Hossain, Lubis, & Ahmed, 2016). Food adulteration is economically motivated, with financial gain being the ultimate goal. Meat products are the frequent target of adulteration; due to its lower cost, horsemeat has become an alternative for beef (Ren et al., 2017). On top of this, screening for genetically modified organisms (GMO) is necessary, due to perceived health concerns by the public, as well as to satisfy legislations requirements (Salihah et al., 2016). As genetically modified plants such as soybean and corn are extensively distributed around the globe (James, 2010), there is a rise in GMO-associated food forgery and mislabeling. The increasing risk of GMO residues unintentionally contaminating non-GMO food during food processing and production, causing the value of the products to depreciate (Ruther, 2009). Therefore, accurate detection of GMOs is crucial to preserve the integrity of food products. In addressing concerns on these issues, various biological markers, such as protein and DNA, have been investigated for food authentication purposes. An inability to withstand high temperature has hindered protein's roles as a marker (Cammà, Di Domenico, & Monaco, 2012; Nakyinsige, Che Man, & Sazili, 2012). In contrast, due to its stability at high temperatures and abundant presence in cells, DNA is rendered a suitable target for detection (Lockley & Bardsley, 2000). As opposed to nuclear or chromosomal DNA, mitochondrial DNA is widely used for identification; the circular shape and protection in the mitochondria confers superior stability. Thus, the structure reduces susceptibility of DNA to degradation (Gefrides & Welch, 2011) and increases the chances of survival in highly processed foods (Mohamad, El Sheikha, anonymous, & Mokhtar, 2013). In animal cells, mitochondrial DNA were packed into five to seven genomes called nucleoid (Bogenhagen, 2009). In addition, single nucleoid carry either one or two molecules of mitochondrial DNA (Gilkerson et al., 2013), which makes it abundant in cells and thus contributes to a higher sensitivity in detection. There are various DNA extraction strategies available, such as chemical, thermal, enzymatic, or mechanical lyses, or a combination of aforementioned methods (Rantakokko-Jalava & Jalava, 2002; Reischl, Linde, Metz, Leppmeier, & Lehn, 2000; Tongeren, Degener, & Harmsen, 2011). Nevertheless, despite various DNA methods available commercially, reviews of suitable methods of DNA extraction from various food matrices are lacking. This paper aims to discuss the complexities of various food matrices and the use of various extraction methods that result in different DNA yields. Approaches in DNA Extraction Method for Food Authentication DNA extraction methods consists of three common steps: lysis, purification, and DNA recovery, with lysis being the most critical step (Barbosa, Nogueira, Gadanho, & Chaves, 2015). In addition, DNA can be extracted using either a conventional method or a commercial extraction kit. A conventional method employs various chemicals, which require preparation prior to the extraction of DNA. However, this method is time consuming and may introduce inhibitors due to the use of certain chemicals during extraction, such as chloroform. Alternatively, DNA extraction methods using a commercial extraction kit is rapid and easy, but expensive. Table 1 shows various DNA separation principles for respective DNA extraction methods. What heat does to DNA structure and detectability

Heat alters DNA structure primarily by denaturing double-stranded DNA (dsDNA), unwinding it into single strands, and potentially fragmenting longer molecules. Direct evidence from the search material shows that heating at high temperatures, such as 95°C, is the most common way to denature dsDNA, especially for PCR, and that denaturation involves unwinding and separating strands detectable by fluorescence [N1-R2]. The same evidence also notes that excessive heat or high pH can damage DNA and break covalent bonds, leading to fragmented or degraded samples [N1-R4]. Another source explains that thermal denaturation of dsDNA is influenced by base stacking, which enhances stability but also sharpens the denaturation transition [N1-R3]. Taken together, this means heat can both melt DNA structure and cause covalent damage, with the exact effect depending on temperature and base composition.

The DNA features most sensitive to thermal damage are the covalent bonds that hold the DNA backbone together, as well as the longer molecular structures that are more vulnerable to fragmentation. The evidence explicitly states that excessive heat can break covalent bonds and that DNA is degraded into small fragments during thermal processing [N1-R4]. It also says that DNA is still detectable even after fragmentation, but fragment size is a limiting factor for subsequent PCR [N5-F1]. In other words, DNA can survive heating, but its ability to be amplified depends on how much it is fragmented. The same source further notes that DNA is largely unaffected by tissue source or sample damage, but fragment size is the main constraint for PCR [N5-F1]. This implies that DNA integrity is more about molecular length and fragmentation than about the source of the sample.

Detectability changes with amplicon length, GC content, and primer design in several ways. Shorter amplicons are easier to amplify and are less affected by fragmentation than longer ones. The search evidence on PCR detection limits states that designing amplicons within the 50–80 bp range can significantly enhance success rates for DNA-based identification [N2-R1]. It also notes that DNA degradation from food processing was characterized using conventional PCR with different target-length amplicons detected on agarose gels [N2-R2]. This suggests that amplicon length is a major determinant of detectability: shorter targets are more likely to remain intact and produce detectable PCR products. GC content is also relevant because PCR primers are typically recommended to have a G+C content of around 50% [N2-R3], which can affect primer binding efficiency and amplification success. The evidence on DNA degradation in processed foods further indicates that DNA fragmentation affects the limit of detection by qualitative PCR, and that effective concentration depends on the amplicon length [N2-F4]. Therefore, primer design and target length should be optimized for fragmented DNA, favoring shorter amplicons and appropriate GC balance to maximize PCR sensitivity.

Overall, heating during food processing primarily denatures dsDNA, fragments longer molecules, and can break covalent bonds, while detectability is strongly limited by amplicon length, GC content, and primer design [N1-R2][N1-R4][N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-F4]. The clearest conclusion is that heat can destroy DNA structure and reduce detectability, but PCR can still work if the amplicon and primer design match the remaining fragment size and thermal damage.
node_outputs.N8:
How food-processing conditions affect DNA integrity in practice

Common food-processing methods include canning, pasteurization, boiling, roasting, baking, and extrusion, each with different thermal profiles. The search material indicates that thermal processing is divided into two main categories: pasteurization and sterilization [N3-R2]. It also gives specific temperature ranges: pasteurization can be at 63–75°C for batch or 72°C for 15 seconds in HTST [N3-R4]. The evidence further notes that the NIST study showed DNA damage in foods when boiled and roasted, and that higher temperatures caused more damage [N3-R3]. This suggests that the thermal profile is a major determinant of DNA impact: higher temperatures and longer exposure tend to increase damage.

The processing durations and temperatures that are most damaging are those that combine high temperature with prolonged exposure. The evidence says that cooking for 5 minutes or more, extrusion at high temperatures and/or high torque settings, and in most processed foods from supermarket shelves caused substantial DNA degradation [N2-F4]. The same source also reports that maize DNA was degraded by cooking, extrusion, and in most processed foods, and that processing reduced the effective concentration of DNA sequences capable of directing amplification of the <100 bp assays, especially after popping corn or extrusion under combined high-temperature and high-torque conditions [N2-F4]. This shows that both temperature and duration matter, but that combined high-temperature/high-torque extrusion is particularly damaging. The NIST study also emphasizes that higher temperatures led to greater DNA damage [N3-R3], reinforcing that temperature is the dominant thermal stressor.

DNA can still be recovered from heat-treated food samples, but recovery is often compromised. The evidence from processed-food DNA extraction indicates that DNA is exposed to heat and physical/chemical treatments, which can degrade DNA molecules [N5-F1]. Despite degradation, DNA is still detectable, but fragment size becomes a limiting factor for PCR [N5-F1]. Another source reports that DNA is largely unaffected by tissue source or sample damage, but fragment size is the main constraint for PCR [N5-F1]. This means that heat-treated DNA is not always completely destroyed, but it is more fragmented and harder to amplify unless the amplicon and primer design are suited to the remaining fragment size. The same evidence also states that DNA is degraded into small fragments during thermal processing, but these are still detectable [N5-F1]. Thus, while heat-treated DNA is often damaged, it can still be recovered and detected, especially if the downstream PCR is designed for short amplicons [N2-F4].

In practical terms, food-processing conditions that are most damaging are those involving high temperature, prolonged exposure, and mechanical force, such as extrusion under high torque and high temperature [N2-F4][N3-R3]. The thermal profiles of common methods are broad, but the most damaging are the ones that push temperature and duration beyond what DNA can tolerate without substantial fragmentation [N3-R2][N3-R4]. DNA recovery is possible, but the quality and usability for PCR depend heavily on the extent of fragmentation [N5-F1][N5-F4]. So the practical conclusion is that heat can severely impair DNA integrity, especially when temperature and duration are high, but detectable DNA can still be obtained if the processing conditions and downstream PCR are matched appropriately.
node_outputs.N9:
How PCR performance is affected by heat-treated food samples

Sample preparation steps that preserve or destroy DNA for PCR are highly important. The evidence shows that DNA extraction is a critical step for species identification by PCR analysis in processed food and feed, and that the quality and yield of DNA are critical for subsequent PCR analysis [N5-F1]. It also notes that DNA is largely unaffected by tissue source or sample damage, but fragment size is a limiting factor for PCR [N5-F1]. In other words, some sample preparation can preserve DNA, but fragmentation from heat treatment can still destroy amplification potential. The same source emphasizes that the chemical compounds present in food matrices may not be completely removed during DNA extraction and can affect DNA integrity or cause PCR inhibition [N5-F1]. This means that careful extraction is needed to preserve DNA and avoid contaminants.

Common contamination and inhibition problems after heat treatment include inhibitors from food matrices, which can interfere with PCR. The evidence explicitly states that inhibitor compounds can decrease or even completely inhibit DNA polymerase activity [N5-F1]. It also says that chemical reagents used in the isolation procedure may persist as contaminants and influence the purity of extracted DNA [N5-F1]. In addition, the contamination review notes that partial inhibition can occur in complex or low-moisture foods due to components such as fats, polyphenols, proteins, and spices [N4-R4]. The same review also links PCR inhibition to humic acids, fulvic acids, fats, and proteins in environmental and food samples [N4-R3]. These inhibitors are especially relevant after heat treatment because thermal processing can expose or concentrate such contaminants, and they can persist through extraction. The evidence on PCR inhibitors also includes a study on DNA heat treatment for reducing inhibition during qPCR analysis of human adenovirus in wastewater samples [N4-R2], suggesting that heating DNA before PCR can help remove inhibitors. This indicates that contamination and inhibition are major practical problems after heat treatment, and that heat can be used strategically in some cases to improve PCR performance.

Interpreting weak or absent PCR results in heat-treated food requires caution. The evidence suggests that DNA degradation from food processing affects the limit of detection by qualitative PCR [N2-F4]. It also says that DNA fragmentation reduces the effective concentration of DNA sequences capable of directing amplification, and that shorter amplicons may still be detectable while longer ones may not [N2-F4]. In addition, the DNA extraction review explains that DNA is exposed to heat and physical/chemical treatments, which can result in DNA degradation, and that the quality and yield of extracted DNA are critical for PCR analysis [N5-F1]. So weak or absent results can come from three main factors: genuine DNA degradation, incomplete removal of inhibitors, or unsuitable amplicon and primer design for fragmented DNA. The real-time PCR fragmentation study further shows that DNA fragmentation affects PCR results and that a fragmentation index can be used to quantify the effect on detection [N5-F2]. This means that a weak PCR result should not be interpreted as a simple “no DNA,” but rather as a signal that thermal damage, inhibitors, or amplicon choice may be limiting amplification. In practice, weak results should be assessed with internal controls, repeated extraction, and consideration of amplicon length and GC content [N2-R3][N2-F4][N5-F1].
node_outputs.N10:
How matrix composition and extraction method affect DNA integrity and PCR outcome

Matrix-specific barriers to DNA recovery in processed foods include complex food matrices, high fragmentation, and persistent inhibitors. The evidence states that DNA analysis of processed foods is performed widely to detect genetically modified organisms and allergens, but that DNA fragmentation caused by physical, chemical, and enzymatic factors can affect PCR analysis [N5-F2]. It also notes that DNA extraction from processed foods is difficult because of the complexity of food matrices, and that DNA extraction often yields insufficient quantities of DNA or causes PCR inhibition by residual impurities [N5-F2]. The review on DNA extraction challenges explains that various food matrices affect DNA extraction, and that DNA can be extracted using conventional or commercial kits, with each approach having different trade-offs in time, cost, and inhibitor handling [N5-F3]. In other words, the food matrix itself is a major barrier: it can reduce DNA yield, increase fragmentation, and introduce inhibitors that interfere with PCR.

Extraction methods that minimize or exacerbate DNA loss vary depending on the matrix. The evidence indicates that commercial kits such as the DNeasy Mericon Food Kit were found to be optimal for DNA extraction from raw muscle, heat-treated muscle, and homemade meat products [N5-F1]. It also says that DNA extraction methods should be optimized for each type of food product because the technological processes used in the food industry can influence DNA quality [N5-F1]. The same source notes that phenol-chloroform extraction gave the highest DNA concentrations, but that this method may not be ideal if the goal is to preserve DNA integrity or avoid inhibitors [N5-F1]. The review further explains that different DNA extraction principles are used, including chemical, thermal, enzymatic, or mechanical lysis, and that the choice of method can affect DNA yield and purity [N5-F3]. This means that some methods minimize loss by preserving DNA, while others exacerbate loss through fragmentation or contamination.

Extraction quality is directly related to downstream PCR sensitivity and specificity. The evidence clearly states that DNA quality and yield are critical for subsequent PCR analysis [N5-F1]. It also notes that DNA is largely unaffected by tissue source or sample damage, but fragment size is a limiting factor for PCR [N5-F1]. In addition, the review on inhibitors says that PCR inhibitors can decrease or completely inhibit DNA polymerase activity [N5-F1], and that contaminants from the isolation procedure can influence extracted DNA purity [N5-F1]. The real-time PCR fragmentation study further shows that DNA fragmentation affects PCR results and that a fragmentation index can quantify the impact on detection [N5-F2]. Therefore, poor extraction quality can reduce PCR sensitivity by fragmenting DNA, introducing inhibitors, or yielding low-quality DNA that fails to amplify. Conversely, high-quality extraction can improve PCR specificity and sensitivity by preserving DNA integrity and minimizing contamination.

In summary, matrix composition creates barriers by increasing fragmentation and introducing inhibitors, while extraction methods can either preserve DNA or worsen loss depending on the approach [N5-F1][N5-F2][N5-F3]. The evidence also shows that extraction quality is central to PCR performance: better extraction improves sensitivity and specificity, whereas poor extraction can reduce both [N5-F1][N5-F2]. So the strongest conclusion is that matrix complexity and extraction method are major determinants of DNA integrity, and that extraction quality should be optimized to maximize downstream PCR success.

Integrated explanation of how heating during food processing impacts DNA integrity and PCR detectability

Heating during food processing generally harms DNA integrity in two main ways: it denatures DNA structure and can fragment longer molecules, and it can also introduce or worsen contaminants that interfere with PCR. The branch reports together show that high-temperature heating is the most common way to denature double-stranded DNA (dsDNA), unwinding it into single strands, while excessive heat or high pH can break covalent bonds and lead to fragmented or degraded samples [N1-R2][N1-R4]. Thermal denaturation is also influenced by base stacking, which can enhance stability but also sharpen the denaturation transition [N1-R3]. So, the direct effect of heat is to weaken DNA structure and increase the likelihood of fragmentation, especially at higher temperatures.

## 1. How heating alters DNA structure and detectability

The clearest conclusion from the branch reports is that heat primarily denatures dsDNA and can fragment longer DNA molecules. It also notes that excessive heat can damage DNA and break covalent bonds, leading to fragmented or degraded samples [N1-R4]. Another source explains that DNA is degraded into small fragments during thermal processing, but these are still detectable [N5-F1]. Taken together, this means that heating can destroy DNA structure, but the remaining DNA can still be amplified if the target is short enough and the PCR conditions are appropriate.

The DNA features most sensitive to thermal damage are the covalent bonds that hold the DNA backbone together and the longer molecular structures that are more vulnerable to fragmentation. The evidence states that DNA is degraded into small fragments during thermal processing [N5-F1], and that fragment size is a limiting factor for PCR [N5-F1]. It also says that DNA is largely unaffected by tissue source or sample damage, but fragment size is the main constraint for PCR [N5-F1]. This implies that the key damage is not the source of the DNA itself, but how much the molecule is fragmented by heat.

Detectability changes with amplicon length, GC content, and primer design. The branch reports show that shorter amplicons are easier to amplify and are less affected by fragmentation than longer ones. Another source notes that DNA degradation from food processing was characterized using conventional PCR with different target-length amplicons detected on agarose gels [N2-R2]. This is important because longer amplicons are more likely to be lost when DNA is fragmented by heat, while shorter amplicons may still be detectable. GC content also matters because PCR primers are typically recommended to have a G+C content of around 50% [N2-R3], which affects primer binding efficiency and amplification success. Finally, the evidence on DNA degradation in processed foods indicates that DNA fragmentation affects the limit of detection by qualitative PCR, and that effective concentration depends on the amplicon length [N2-F4]. So, primer design and amplicon length should be optimized for fragmented DNA, favoring shorter targets and appropriate GC balance to maximize PCR sensitivity.

## 2. How food-processing conditions affect DNA integrity in practice

Common food-processing methods include canning, pasteurization, boiling, roasting, baking, and extrusion. Sample preparation steps that preserve or destroy DNA for PCR are highly important. The evidence shows that DNA extraction is a critical step for species identification by PCR analysis in processed food and feed, and that the quality and yield of DNA are critical for subsequent PCR analysis [N5-F1]. It also notes that DNA is largely unaffected by tissue source or sample damage, but fragment size is a limiting factor for PCR [N5-F1]. In other words, some sample preparation can preserve DNA, but fragmentation from heat treatment can still destroy amplification potential. The evidence explicitly states that inhibitor compounds can decrease or even completely inhibit DNA polymerase activity [N5-F1]. Heating during food processing primarily denatures dsDNA, fragments longer molecules, and can introduce or worsen contaminants that inhibit PCR.
